items.followUp: Differentiate between a scientific theory and a scientific law.

rubric.why: A law describes a natural phenomenon in a concise form.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a law is a concise statement describing a natural phenomenon.

rubric.why: A principle is a general rule supported by scientific observations or experiments.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying a principle as a general rule based on scientific observations or experiments.

modelAnswer: A law is a concise statement that describes a natural phenomenon.
A principle is a general rule based on scientific observations and experiments.

items.followUp: Differentiate between grana and stroma in a chloroplast.

rubric.why: Thylakoids are flattened membrane sacs that contain chlorophyll.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying thylakoids as chlorophyll-containing sacs or membranes.

rubric.why: The stroma is the fluid matrix containing enzymes in the chloroplast.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the stroma as the fluid matrix, preferably noting its enzymes.

modelAnswer: Thylakoids are flattened membrane sacs containing chlorophyll; they are arranged in stacks called grana.
The stroma is the fluid matrix of the chloroplast, containing enzymes, in which the grana are embedded.

items.followUp: How does a light microscope differ from an electron microscope?

rubric.why: A transmission electron microscope (TEM) passes electrons through a thin specimen to show internal details.
rubric.description: Explains how TEM forms an image.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that electrons pass through a thin specimen and reveal its internal structure.

rubric.why: A scanning electron microscope (SEM) scans the specimen's surface to show its surface structure.
rubric.description: Explains how SEM forms an image.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that SEM scans the surface of a specimen.

modelAnswer: A transmission electron microscope (TEM) passes electrons through a thin specimen and shows its internal details.
A scanning electron microscope (SEM) scans the specimen's surface and shows its surface details, usually as a three-dimensional image.

items.followUp: State two differences between the five-kingdom and two-kingdom classification systems.

rubric.why: The two-kingdom system does not separate prokaryotes from eukaryotes.
rubric.description: Gives one defect of the system.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it does not distinguish prokaryotic organisms from eukaryotic organisms.

rubric.why: Fungi were grouped with plants despite lacking chlorophyll and not making their own food like plants.
rubric.description: Gives another defect of the system.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for noting that fungi were classified with plants even though they lack chlorophyll.

modelAnswer: The two-kingdom system does not distinguish between prokaryotes and eukaryotes.
It grouped fungi with plants, although fungi lack chlorophyll.

items.followUp: Why are mules generally unable to produce offspring?

rubric.why: A mule is a hybrid produced by a horse and a donkey.
rubric.description: Identifies the mule as a hybrid.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a mule is a horse–donkey hybrid.

rubric.why: Mules are generally sterile and cannot produce offspring, so they cannot form a reproducing species.
rubric.description: Explains why a mule is not classified as a species.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking its sterility or inability to reproduce to species classification.

modelAnswer: A mule is a hybrid offspring of a horse and a donkey.
Mules are generally sterile and cannot reproduce; therefore, they do not form a species.

items.followUp: Describe how a cell plate forms during cytokinesis in a plant cell.

rubric.why: The cell plate begins to form between the daughter nuclei in the middle of the cell.
rubric.description: States where the cell plate forms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the cell plate forms between the daughter nuclei or in the middle of the cell.

rubric.why: The cell plate develops into a new cell wall and separates the daughter cells.
rubric.description: States the function of the cell plate.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that it forms a new wall or separates the two daughter cells.

modelAnswer: During plant-cell cytokinesis, the cell plate (guided by the phragmoplast) forms between the daughter nuclei.
It grows outwards and develops into a new cell wall, separating the two daughter cells.

items.followUp: State two ways in which mitosis is important for an organism's growth and repair.

rubric.why: Mitosis produces new cells to replace worn-out, damaged or dead cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning replacement of worn-out, damaged or dead cells.

rubric.why: Mitosis produces daughter cells with the same chromosome number as the parent cell, supporting continued cell replacement.
rubric.description: States the result of replacement by mitosis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that mitosis maintains chromosome number or produces genetically identical daughter cells.

modelAnswer: Mitosis replaces worn-out, damaged or dead cells with new cells.
The daughter cells have the same chromosome number as the parent cell, maintaining the organism's tissues.

items.followUp: Give one example of a diploid cell and one example of a haploid cell.

rubric.why: Body or somatic cells are examples of diploid cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving a body or somatic cell as a diploid example.

rubric.why: Gametes, such as sperm or egg cells, are examples of haploid cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving a gamete, sperm or egg cell as a haploid example.

modelAnswer: A gamete, such as a sperm or egg cell, is haploid (n).
